newsitem.title: NIGERIA: African human rights team plans visit to Nigeria.
newsitem.headline: African human rights team plans visit to Nigeria.

text.p: An African human rights team is expected to arrive Nigeria on Friday, a week after United Nations envoys cancelled a similar mission, local rights activists said on Wednesday.

State-run News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) quoted a presidency source as saying that the three-man team, from the Gambia-based African Commission on Human Rights and People's Rights, was coming at the invitation of the military government.

The delegation would stay until March 14 and meet with government officials, members of the transition implementation agencies, national human rights commission, non-governmental organisations and individuals, the agency said.

It said the team would visit the cities of Abuja, Lagos, Port-Harcourt, Kaduna and Kano and would be led by Ghanaian E.V.O. Dankwah. The others are Togolese Atsu Koffi-Amega and Essombe Joseph, a legal officer of the commission.
Earlier, Abdul Oroh, executive director of the Civil Liberties Organisation (CLO), Nigeria's leading human rights group, said of the delegation: "They have been trying to come for almost a year."
The U.N. mission called off their visit last week after the military government refused them access to jails and detainees.

Oroh and local newspapers said the government agreed to allow the African team to see detainees including presidential claimant Moshood Abiola, 19 youths from the Ogoni minority tribe who are detained over the 1994 murder of four Ogoni chiefs as well as human rights groups.

The Ogoni youths face the death penalty like executed author Ken Saro-Wiwa, who was hanged with eight other Ogoni minority rights activists in 1995 over the same murders after a trial condemned internationally as unfair.
The U.N. mission had been due to report back to the U.N. Human Rights Commission, which opens its annual session on March 10 when Nigeria is expected to be in the dock for rights abuses.

The CLO and the Constitutional Rights Project, another Nigerian human rights group, in a joint letter to the missioners protested against the inclusion of Amega, who led a U.N. mission to Nigeria last year and endorsed the military's transition plan.
"We are concerned that Mr Koffi Amega's inclusion in the mission already taints its objectivity," said their letter, which was released to the media.
